label: Differential Forms
notes: Open by stating the goal: forms are the algebra that makes integration coordinate free and that later carries the symplectic structure. Stress that a k-form is a machine eating k vectors and returning an oriented number, and that the whole appendix builds toward one Stokes identity unifying grad, curl, and divergence.

label: Alternating Forms
notes: Define an alternating k-form on a vector space as a multilinear map that flips sign under any swap of two arguments. Emphasize the consequence: feeding a repeated vector gives zero, so forms detect linear independence. The space of k-forms has dimension n choose k, vanishing once k exceeds the dimension.

label: The Wedge Product
notes: Introduce the wedge as the antisymmetrized tensor product producing a higher-degree form. Drill the two rules learners forget: anticommutativity up to a sign from degrees, and that a one-form wedged with itself is zero. Connect to determinants now, since that is the meaning unlocked on the next slide.

label: Oriented Volume
notes: Show the 2-form built from two one-forms returns the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the input vectors, computed as a two by two determinant. Walk the diagram: swapping the inputs reverses orientation and flips the sign. This is the seed of every flux and volume integral that follows.

label: Differential Forms on Manifolds
notes: Promote algebraic forms to fields: a differential k-form assigns an alternating form to each point, written in the coordinate basis of wedged differentials. Functions are zero-forms. Stress that the coefficients are smooth functions and that this object is exactly what we will integrate over surfaces and chains.

label: The Exterior Derivative
notes: Define d as the unique operator raising degree by one, linear, obeying a graded Leibniz rule, and reducing to the ordinary differential on functions. Give the coordinate formula: differentiate each coefficient and wedge. Preview that in three dimensions d reproduces gradient, curl, and divergence in turn.

label: d squared equals zero
notes: State the central identity that applying d twice annihilates any form, rooted in equality of mixed partial derivatives. Translate it to vector calculus: curl of a gradient and divergence of a curl both vanish. This single fact is what makes closed and exact forms, and de Rham cohomology, even possible.

label: Pullback of Forms
notes: Explain that a smooth map pulls forms backward, substituting the map into the coordinates and differentials. Highlight the two clean properties: pullback commutes with the wedge and with the exterior derivative. This is precisely what lets us change variables inside an integral without tracking Jacobians by hand.

label: Integration over Chains
notes: Define integrating a k-form over an oriented k-chain by pulling back to a parameter domain and integrating the coefficient. Stress orientation: reversing it negates the integral. Chains are formal sums of oriented cells, and their boundary operator, which we meet next, is dual to the exterior derivative.

label: The General Stokes Theorem
notes: State the master theorem: the integral of d omega over a region equals the integral of omega over its oriented boundary. Read it as a duality pairing d against the boundary operator. Every classical integral theorem is one instance; show learners the shape before naming the special cases.

label: Green, Gauss, Kelvin-Stokes
notes: Specialize the master identity. A one-form on a planar region gives Green's theorem; a two-form flux in space with d acting as divergence gives Gauss; circulation of a one-form around a curve bounding a surface gives Kelvin-Stokes. One statement, three familiar theorems, each chosen by the degree of the form.

label: Closed, Exact, Cohomology
notes: Close by defining closed forms as those killed by d and exact forms as those that are themselves a d of something. Since d squared is zero, every exact form is closed; the failure of the converse measures the holes of the space. That quotient is de Rham cohomology, and this language now carries the symplectic form.
